summary: This standards-track document specifies algorithm identifiers and ASN.1 encoding formats for elliptic curve constructs using curve25519 and curve448 in X.509. It covers the Ed25519 and Ed448 signature algorithms and the X25519 and X448 key agreement algorithms, including public and private key encodings.

plainLanguage.summary: Certificates need to say which math tools they use. This gives the official names for some modern, popular ones.

subtitle: The object identifiers and encodings that let X.509 certificates carry Ed25519, Ed448, X25519 and X448 keys.

tldr.problem: Certificates need a standard way to say that a key or signature uses curve25519 or curve448, and the curves had no X.509 identifiers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four object identifiers, id-X25519, id-X448, id-Ed25519 and id-Ed448, with absent parameters. It also fixes how public keys, private keys and EdDSA signatures are encoded.
tldr.outcome: Certificates and key files can carry these modern curves in a consistent way. The RFC is updated by RFC 9295.

today: RFC 8410 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9295. It covers only the PureEdDSA mode and does not define contexts or the prehash variants.

sections.title: Why These Identifiers Are Needed
sections.content:
RFC 7748 describes the elliptic curves curve25519 and curve448, which are designed with performance and security in mind. Used for Diffie-Hellman they are called X25519 and X448. RFC 8032 describes the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA), which has a PureEdDSA mode without prehashing and a HashEdDSA mode with prehashing. The names Ed25519 and Ed448 identify the PureEdDSA mode.

This document defines the ASN.1 object identifiers (OIDs) and parameters for these four algorithms and describes how they are used for public keys, private keys and, for the EdDSA ones, signatures. It does not cover the prehash versions.

It also leaves out EdDSA contexts. The stated reasons are that current Ed25519 implementations do not support them, that EdDSA is the only IETF algorithm with contexts and that could cause confusion about which algorithms need separate keys, that the cryptographic community is still debating how effective contexts are, and that it is unclear how to identify when a context string is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Two famous math recipes for locking and signing already existed. This document gives each one an official name tag so a certificate can say which recipe it uses.

sections.title: The Four Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content:
A certificate that follows RFC 5280 says which public key algorithm it uses through an AlgorithmIdentifier, which is an OID plus optional parameters. This document defines four new OIDs for the curve and algorithm pairs, and for all of them the parameters MUST be absent.

The RFC admits some systems demand the parameters be present, because of a defect in the original 1997 syntax or a programming error. Its advice is to fix those systems, and where that is impossible to confine the problem to that subsystem and not spread it across the Internet.

The same identifiers are used for a public key, a private key and, for the two EdDSA OIDs, a signature.
sections.plainLanguage: Each recipe gets a short numeric code, like a library call number. The code stands alone, with nothing extra written next to it.

sections.title: Public Keys and Key Usage
sections.content:
In an X.509 certificate the subjectPublicKeyInfo field holds an algorithm (the identifier above) and a subjectPublicKey BIT STRING with the public key bytes. These algorithms always encode the public key as an exact multiple of 8 bits. The public key is computed differently in RFC 7748 and RFC 8032, so the same private key does not produce the same public key. Keys can be shown in the textual encoding from RFC 7468.

The keyUsage extension says what a key is for. If it is present with id-X25519 or id-X448, then keyAgreement MUST be present, and encipherOnly or decipherOnly MAY also be present. If it is present in an end-entity certificate with id-Ed25519 or id-Ed448, it MUST contain nonRepudiation, digitalSignature or both. In a certification authority certificate with those OIDs, it MUST contain one or more of nonRepudiation, digitalSignature, keyCertSign and cRLSign.
sections.plainLanguage: The key goes in a labeled box inside the certificate. The certificate also says what the key may be used for, such as signing or agreeing on a secret.

sections.title: EdDSA Signatures and Private Keys
sections.content:
For signatures, the same algorithm identifiers are used and the parameters MUST be absent. The data to sign is prepared for EdDSA, then a private key operation produces the signature, which is the opaque value ENC(R) || ENC(S) from Section 3.3 of RFC 8032. It goes directly into the BIT STRING with no extra ASN.1 wrapping. In a certificate it fills the signatureValue field.

Private keys use the OneAsymmetricKey structure from RFC 5958. For these keys the private key is an opaque byte sequence, held in a CurvePrivateKey, which is an OCTET STRING, and wrapped inside the privateKey OCTET STRING. The publicKey field is optional. The RFC notes that some private key import functions do not accept a structure with the public key field, so implementers must balance a consistency check on the key pair against the widest ability to import the key.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature is just a stamp that is placed as is in a slot. A private key is wrapped in a plain envelope, optionally with a copy of the matching public key tucked in.

sections.title: Names, Examples and Invalid Encodings
sections.content:
For consistent naming, implementations SHOULD use these human-readable names. Use ECDH for an X25519 or X448 public key when the curve is not known or relevant, and X25519 or X448 when it is known. Use EdDSA for a signing public key or signature when the curve is not known or relevant, and Ed25519 or Ed448 when it is.

The RFC includes an ASN.1 module, an example Ed25519 public key, a self-issued certificate where Ed25519 signs an X25519 public key, and Ed25519 private key examples with and without the public key and an attribute.

Appendix A lists invalid encodings an importer must handle. These are ASN.1 errors, such as using an OCTET STRING instead of a BIT STRING for the public key, or a wrong version value (0 if the publicKey is absent, 1 if present). Others are key encoding errors, such as an X25519 key that breaks the masking rules, and key mismatch errors. It also shows a valid BER encoding that many systems may not accept because they decode only DER.
sections.plainLanguage: The document also gives sample certificates and keys to copy from, and a list of broken samples so programs learn to spot a bad key.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5280, RFC 7748 and RFC 8032 apply. The only additional point is that the steps from private key to public key differ for Diffie-Hellman and for Edwards signatures, so the same public key cannot be used for both ECDH and EdDSA.

For IANA, the ASN.1 module got value 93 for id-mod-safecurves-pkix in the SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier registry. The OIDs themselves are registered independently, per RFC 8411.
sections.plainLanguage: A key made for signing should not also be used for secret handshakes. They are made in different ways, so each key keeps one job.
